name: Name
body: Battle Forge is a monthly series that presents a new WARMACHINE scenario in each installment. Battle Forge scenarios emphasize the narrative unfolding over the course of a game and may be asymmetrical, uneven, and even somewhat experimental because the goal of Battle Forge is to create a sandbox toolset that allows for creative scenario generation and new, story-worthy experiences with WARMACHINE! Players are encouraged to modify Battle Forge scenarios in any way that makes the scenario more appropriate for their army collections and their available terrain resources. Most important of all, have fun! And if you find a better way to do something with a scenario that results in a better experience for you, let us know at feedback@privateerpress.com, so we can try it, too!

name: Name
body: Following are the key terms that will be repeated in many Battle Forge scenarios:

name: Name
body: Many scenarios utilize objectives. An objective can either be a terrain piece, a marker, or a zone designated on a terrain piece or on the map.

name: Name
body: Objective Markers are impassable terrain features and should be represented on the table with markers that are at least 20 mm in diameter. Unless otherwise specified, all Objective Markers used in a scenario should be the same size.

name: Name
body: To have more models in an area than your opponent does.

name: Name
body: An area or objective is contested if both players have models in the area or in scoring proximity to the objective at a time when scoring would take place. An area or objective is uncontested if only one player has models in the area or in scoring proximity to the objective when scoring would take place.

name: Name
body: The zone or the area of a terrain feature is held when a player occupies the area with two or more models, uncontested.

name: Name
body: An objective terrain piece or marker is secured when a player has two or more models within 1" of the objective, uncontested.

name: Name
body: Battle Forge victories can be determined by either achieving the goals of the scenario or through Victory Points, scored in a variety of ways throughout playing a scenario. Turn limits on scenarios put pressure on players to succeed within a set amount of turns, and Victory Points provide the means to determine victory when neither player has completed the primary objective of a scenario.

name: Name
body: In addition to its standard rules, each Battle Forge scenario has two random tables that add additional Victory Point-scoring opportunities for players that vary each time the scenario is played. Mission Modifiers add additional scoring opportunities based on the position of a player’s models on the table. Achievements add additional scoring opportunities based on a player’s actions taken on the battlefield. Players should roll a d6 to randomly determine Mission Modifiers and Achievements before the beginning of a game, or players can choose them at will if all players agree. It is recommended that only one Mission Modifier and one Achievement should be in effect during any match (unless you really want to get crazy).

name: Name
body: If a player makes an attack that destroys one or more friendly models, that player’s opponent gains 1 Victory Point. If a player makes an attack and destroys their own Leader model, that player immediately loses the match.

name: Name
body: In addition to objectives, Battle Forge scenarios will routinely draw on the following terrain elements. Dimensions provided are approximations, and you should feel free to substitute any terrain pieces you have available as necessary. Use the resources you have available to get close enough to maintain the spirit and intention of the scenario.

name: Name
body: An obstacle with an approximate footprint of 3/4" x 4". Barriers provide cover.

name: Name
body: Obstructions with an approximate footprint of 5" x 5".

name: Name
body: Forest areas with an approximate footprint of 5" in diameter.

name: Name
body: An obstacle with an approximate footprint of 2" x 2". Small obstacles provide cover.

name: Name
body: An elevated platform at least 1" above the table, such as a hill or terrace. Plateaus can possess multiple areas at different heights that models can be placed on, but the areas must be level to prevent models from falling over. If a model cannot be placed on a level area without risk of falling off, it cannot occupy that area. Models cannot be placed on slopes, and we recommend that plateau terrain with sloped surfaces not be used. Hill, Small—A plateau platform with a footprint approximately 6" in diameter and a level surface(s) at least 1" above the table that is large enough for five 30 mm models to be placed on. Hill, Large—A plateau with a footprint approximately 6" to 12" in diameter and a level surface(s) at least 1" above the table that is large enough for five 40 mm models to be placed on.

name: Name
body: An area of shallow water approximately 6" in diameter.

name: Name
body: An area of rubble approximately 6" in diameter.

name: Name
body: A 3" x 5" trench template.

name: Name
body: Their allies were desperate for supplies—ammunition, medicines, and food—that would keep them going for another fortnight in their battle to hold off the invaders from their homeland. All that stood between the defenders and the safe delivery of their precious cargo was a band of savages and one last treacherous stretch of unforgiving road.

name: Name
body: "Fury Road" is designed to be played with 50- or 75-point forces.

name: Name
body: "Fury Road" ends after eight rounds.

name: Name
body: One player attempts to move a mobile cargo objective through a treacherous course to get it to safety while the other player attacks from all directions in a battle to stop them from delivering that cargo.

name: Name
body:
If Player 1 delivers the cargo to the safe zone, that player wins the match.
If Player 2 prevents delivery of the cargo to the safe zone before the round limit is met, that player wins the match.

name: Name
body:
The map shown uses several hills, rubble, and forests as well as multiple walls. But use whatever terrain you have available to create a hazardous, canyon-like path that will prevent the cargo from being moved off of it.
You will also need two respawn objectives to place near the center of the table and four more rally point objectives to place around the edges of the table to represent secondary deployment points for Player 2.
Last, you’ll need a mobile cargo objective with a 50 mm base.

name: Name
body:
This scenario uses Execution Mode.
During deployment, Player 1 deploys their models first and must place the mobile cargo objective anywhere completely in their deployment zone.
Player 2 deploys only their Leader model, Cohort models in its battlegroup, and immobile models that do not have a SPD stat, like structures, before the start of the game. The rest of Player 2’s forces are held in reserve.
After the first turn, Player 2 can put up to three models/units from their reserve into play, placing them anywhere completely within 3" of any rally point objective or anywhere in that player’s original deployment zone.
If Player 1 begins their turn securing a rally point objective, the objective is removed from the table.
If Player 2 begins their turn securing a respawn objective, the objective is removed from the table, and Player 2 can return one destroyed unit or solo to their reserves.
Only Player 1 can move the mobile cargo objective.
When a medium- or large-based Cohort model begins its activation within 1" of the mobile cargo objective, it can place the objective within 1" of the Cohort model after it has moved and as long as the Cohort model did not run, slam, or charge. The mobile cargo objective can only be moved during normal movement. The mobile cargo objective can be moved multiple times in a single turn if more than one Cohort model begins its activation within 1" of the objective.

name: Name
body:
The mobile cargo objective cannot be placed by a Cohort model that moved through hill, plateau, or forest terrain or over obstacles during its activation.
Player 1 gains 1 Victory Point every time they begin their turn securing a rally point objective.
Player 2 gains 1 Victory Point every time they begin their turn securing the mobile cargo objective.

name: Name
body: Roll once on both the Mission Modifiers and Achievement tables.

name: Name
body: Roll a d3 to determine the Mission Modifier for this match. 1. Rolling Fog—Roll a d6 before each of Player 1’s turns. On a 1–2, all models on hills or plateaus gain Stealth. On a 3–4, all models that are not on hills or plateaus gain Stealth. On a 5–6, all models gain Stealth. This result lasts for one round. 2. Sand Storms—Models on hills or plateaus suffer –2 to RAT. 3. Flash Floods—Roll a d6 before each of Player 1’s turns. On a six, all terrain that is not a hill or plateau is considered rough terrain for one round.

name: Name
body: Roll a d3 to determine the Achievement for this match. 1. Speedster—The first player whose Leader model crosses to their opponent’s side of the table gains 1 Victory Point. 2. First Blood—The first player to damage their opponent’s Leader with an attack made by their own Leader gains 1 Victory Point. 3. Big Game Hunter—The first player to destroy their opponent’s Cohort model gains 1 Victory Point.

name: Name
body: Victory conditions are checked in the following order: Decisive Win: If Player 1 delivers the mobile cargo objective to the safe zone by the end of their eighth turn, they win the match. If they do not, or because of attrition cannot, then Player 2 wins the match. Point Advantage Win: At the end of any of the second player’s turns, if a player has 4 or more Victory Points than their opponent, they win the match. Last Leader Win: At the end of any of the second player’s turns, a player with the last Leader model in play wins the match. Victory Point Win: If neither player has a Leader in play at the end of any of the second player’s turns, the player with the most Victory Points wins the match.
